request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Chinese restaurant team leader, male, 7th year

Interviewer: How does your manager usually get on with everyone?

Interviewee: The biggest thing about our manager is that he loves telling cold jokes, the really corny kind. He tells one at the morning briefing every single day, and when he’s finished he’s the first to laugh. For example, he says: why can’t eggs tell jokes? Because they’d crack up. Not one person in the room laughs. He’s the only one there enjoying himself. I’ve told him several times: boss, that joke really isn’t funny, could you stop telling them, you’re wasting everyone’s time. He says no, it’s his tradition. The morning briefing is only meant to be ten minutes, and we have to cover that day’s bookings, dishes that have sold out and special requests for the private rooms. One joke plus his explanation takes up three or four minutes, so everything after that has to be rushed. Several times new staff didn’t catch the allergy requests for the private rooms, and there were near misses when serving. Once a guest was allergic to peanuts and the server for that private room didn’t hear. The cold starter almost went out with peanuts in it. Luckily the runner stopped it. I formally raised it once at a department meeting and asked whether the briefing could cover the actual business first and leave the joke till the end. He said he’d consider it, and the next day he told one first as usual. After that a few of the long-serving staff just started turning up five minutes late, coming in after he’d finished, and he said we weren’t showing him any respect. I don’t think this is about respect. It’s about what the morning briefing is actually for. Last time head office came to do an employee satisfaction survey, I wrote this in the comments box. I was very specific, and even wrote down which day there’d been a near miss. So, our manager isn’t a bad person, it’s just that his jokes are too cold, and he won’t listen. I really can’t stand him.
